title: The Letter Mostafa Kandil Sent Two Months After Swvl Went Public
dek: In May 2022 Swvl's chief executive cut a third of his staff to save cash; by the end of the year half the rest had gone, and so had most of its markets.

story.event: Cutting staff and markets in 2022 after a fast global expansion and a Nasdaq listing
story.summary: On 30 May 2022, two months after Swvl listed on Nasdaq through a SPAC merger valuing it at $1.5 billion, chief executive Mostafa Kandil announced a programme to cut about 32% of staff and focus on its most profitable operations. In November it cut half of its remaining staff, shut its Pakistan operations and concentrated on its largest markets, and over the following year it unwound or sold most of its acquisitions. Narrowed to a business-to-business company in a few markets, it reported a net profit for 2023 on sharply lower revenue.
paragraphs: On 30 May 2022, two months after Swvl began trading on Nasdaq, its co-founder and chief executive, Mostafa Kandil, wrote to his staff. The Cairo-born, Dubai-based mass-transit company would cut about 32% of its workforce, roughly 400 people. "To those who will leave, I would like to say I am sorry. And more importantly, this is not your fault," he wrote.

Kandil, Mahmoud Nouh and Ahmed Sabbah had started Swvl in Egypt in 2017 to let commuters book seats on buses running fixed routes. In the year before the letter it had moved fast: a merger with the blank-cheque company Queen's Gambit at a $1.5 billion valuation, purchases of Viapool in Argentina, Shotl in Spain, Volt Lines in Turkey and Germany's door2door, a planned deal for Britain's Zeelo, and talk of entering Colombia, Mexico, South Africa and the United States. By late May the shares, listed at about $10, had traded mostly between $4 and $8 as tech valuations fell.

Kandil called his answer a portfolio optimisation programme. Consumer bus routes would concentrate on Egypt and Pakistan, its strongest consumer markets, while contracts with businesses and transport operators, worth over $5 million a month, kept growing. Senior managers took voluntary pay cuts, hiring and travel were frozen and office space was reduced. "No matter how big, resources are not infinite," he wrote. The goal was positive cash flow in 2023. Swvl's finance chief told TechCrunch it was not leaving any country.

That did not hold. In July the Zeelo deal was called off. In November Swvl cut half of its remaining staff, said it would focus on its largest markets, chiefly Egypt and Mexico, and weighed selling or closing smaller ones; Pakistan, its second-largest market by revenue, had just been shut. The shares were below $1. Over the next year it unwound the Volt Lines purchase and sold or closed subsidiaries in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Germany and Pakistan.

What remained was a much smaller business-to-business company, working mainly in Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Helped by those sales, it reported a net profit of $3.1 million for 2023 while revenue fell by almost half. By 2026 it was growing again in seven countries, including the United States, and described itself as approaching operating breakeven.

quote.text: Did you ever think what those sleepers are that underlie the railroad? Each one is a man, an Irish-man, or a Yankee man. The rails are laid on them, and they are covered with sand, and the cars run smoothly over them.
quote.locator: Chapter 2, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"
quote.source_title: Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, Project Gutenberg eBook #205
quote.connection: Thoreau's sleepers are the railway's wooden ties and the labourers who laid them, unseen beneath a smooth ride. Swvl's speed and its correction were both carried by people who had not set the pace. Kandil's apology names that cost; Thoreau would ask whether naming it is the same as weighing it before the rails go down.

reflection: Much of what Kandil cut in 2022 had been bought within the year before. The letter is decent: it apologises, it says plainly that the people leaving were not at fault. But the more useful lesson sits earlier, in the months when every new market looked like progress and nobody had to say what it would cost to undo.

You will make promises to people as you build, about their jobs, their time, what you will deliver to them. Each one is easier to make than to take back. Growth that you can carry on a tired Tuesday is worth more than growth that only holds when markets are kind.
invitation: Before you take on one new commitment this week, write one sentence on what it would cost you, and the person on the other side, if you had to undo it in six months.

sources.title: Swvl plans to lay off 32% of its team two months after going public (Tage Kene-Okafor, 30 May 2022)
sources.supports: The 30 May 2022 announcement of a 32% cut; about 1,330 employees on LinkedIn, so around 400 jobs; listing at $10 and trading between $4 and $8; five acquisitions within the year; target of positive cash flow in 2023; more than $5 million monthly revenue from TaaS and SaaS; extracts of Kandil's letter, including 'No matter how big, resources are not infinite' and 'To those who will leave, I would like to say I am sorry. And more importantly, this is not your fault'; CFO Youssef Salem's statement that Swvl was not shutting down operations in any country.

sources.title: All eyes are on Swvl as it starts trading on a SPAC combination (31 March 2022)
sources.supports: Listing on Nasdaq through a merger with Queen's Gambit Growth Capital at a $1.5 billion valuation; founded in 2017 by Mostafa Kandil, Mahmoud Nouh and Ahmed Sabbah as a bus-hailing service with seats on fixed routes; acquisitions of Shotl, Viapool and door2door; plans to expand into Colombia, Mexico, South Africa and the US.

sources.title: Swvl's $100M acquisition of smart bus startup Zeelo is off amid tech stocks slump (29 July 2022)
sources.supports: The Zeelo acquisition announced in April 2022 was terminated in July 2022 amid falling markets.

sources.title: Swvl reduces its headcount by 50% six months after axing 400 staff (28 November 2022)
sources.supports: Second round of layoffs affecting 50% of the remaining headcount; focus on largest markets including Egypt and Mexico; evaluation of sale, scale-back or discontinuation in smaller markets; presence in 20 markets as of June 2022; share price of about $0.40 and a Nasdaq compliance notice; H1 2022 revenue of $40.7 million and losses of $161.6 million.

sources.title: Mobility startup SWVL shuts operations in Pakistan, its second biggest market (Taimoor Hassan, 24 November 2022)
sources.supports: Swvl shut its intercity and TaaS verticals in Pakistan on 17 and 18 November 2022 after pausing retail service in June; Pakistan was its second-biggest market by revenue ($9.71 million of about $40 million in H1 2022); net loss of $161.6 million for H1 2022; Kandil did not respond to requests for comment.

sources.title: SWVL to lay off 32 per cent of its workforce, expects to turn profitable in 2023 (May 2022)
sources.supports: Text of Swvl's press release: reduction of headcount by about 32%; B2C business to focus on Egypt and Pakistan, its highest B2C revenue and profitability markets; continued TaaS and SaaS growth across all markets with more than $5 million monthly revenue; expectation of positive cash flow in 2023.

sources.title: SWVL slashes over 50 per cent of its workforce, shuts operations in Pakistan (November 2022)
sources.supports: Over 50% of staff laid off in the second round; Pakistan shut; focus on Egypt and Mexico; evaluation of sale, scale-back or discontinuation of smaller markets; cuts to marketing and third-party spending; shares at about $0.40 against a $9.95 listing price.

sources.title: Egypt's Swvl lays off a third of its staff two months after going public (31 May 2022)
sources.supports: Cut of about 400 people (CFO Youssef Salem to Bloomberg) announced in Kandil's letter of 30 May; the 'resources are not infinite' line; voluntary salary deductions for top management, reduced office space, hiring freeze and cuts to travel; presence in 13 markets in May 2022.

sources.title: Swvl wants to undo its Volt Lines acquisition as it struggles (25 January 2023)
sources.supports: Swvl agreed to unwind its 2022 acquisition of Volt Lines; Nasdaq compliance warnings; review of strategic alternatives.

sources.title: Swvl's acquisition of Volt Lines came to a halt (January 2023)
sources.supports: The Volt Lines takeover, announced in April 2022 at $40 million, was unwound in December 2022, effective 6 January 2023, because of Swvl's falling share price and financial constraints.

sources.title: NASDAQ-listed Swvl engineers a reversal of fortune as it finally achieves profitability (5 January 2024)
sources.supports: Profit achieved by selling subsidiaries and narrowing to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE; transition to a B2B company; subsidiaries in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Germany and Pakistan shut or sold.

sources.title: Swvl posts first full-year profit in 2023 (1 May 2024)
sources.supports: Net profit of $3.1 million in 2023 against a net loss of $123.6 million in 2022; revenue down 48% to $22.8 million; operations in Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

sources.title: Swvl secures $13 million investment led by Sawiris-backed Coefficient (August 2026)
sources.supports: In 2026 Swvl operated in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, the UK and the US, had just started US operations, grew first-quarter 2026 revenue by 68% and described itself as approaching operating breakeven.

cross_checks.claim: On 30 May 2022 Swvl announced it would cut about 32% of its workforce, around 400 people, two months after listing.
Swvl listed on Nasdaq through a SPAC merger with Queen's Gambit at a $1.5 billion valuation, at about $10 a share.
In November 2022 Swvl cut about half of its remaining staff, shut Pakistan and focused on its largest markets, with shares below $1.
Swvl unwound its Volt Lines acquisition.
Swvl narrowed to a business-to-business company in a few markets (Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE) and later grew again.

research_notes: Headcount: the 32% cut was put at about 400 people by TechCrunch (from roughly 1,330 LinkedIn profiles) and by the CFO to Bloomberg (via TechCabal); the second round was '50% of its remaining headcount' (TechCrunch, citing Swvl's statement) or 'over 50 per cent' (Wamda), leaving 'a little over 450' by TechCrunch's LinkedIn estimate. The story uses 32%, about 400 and half of the rest, and gives no final headcount. Markets: TechCrunch and TechCabal listed 13 markets in May 2022; Swvl's June 2022 financial statement (via TechCrunch and Pakistan Today) listed 20; the story names no total. Listing price: $10 (TechCrunch, March) vs $9.95 (TechCrunch and Wamda, November); story says 'about $10'. First-half 2022 revenue: $40.7 million (TechCrunch) or about $40 million (Pakistan Today), but TechCabal (January 2023) says $66 million; the story gives no H1 revenue. Volt Lines: TechCabal says the unwinding was filed in January 2023, Wamda that it was agreed in December 2022 and effective 6 January 2023; the story says 'over the next year'. Profit: TechCabal reports a 2023 net profit of $3.1 million on revenue down 48% to $22.8 million, achieved largely through the sale of subsidiaries; Wamda (2026) quotes Swvl describing itself as approaching operating breakeven in 2026, so the story attributes the 2023 profit partly to those sales and does not call the business profitable today. TechCabal's reference to a reverse split in 'January 2022' appears to be a slip for January 2023 and is not used. Kandil's letter was published by Swvl at regular.swvl.com/ceo-letter, which no longer loads; it is quoted from TechCrunch's extract. The Pakistan closure came from company sources to Profit; Swvl's own November statement did not name Pakistan. Setting: Swvl was founded in Cairo but was Dubai-based by the time of its listing (TechCrunch, March 2022), and the layoffs fell mostly on its Dubai and Pakistan offices (TechCrunch), so country is the United Arab Emirates and region Middle East rather than the slate's Egypt and North Africa; Egypt remained its largest market. The Thoreau passage concerns the railway labourers of his day and is applied by analogy.
